phonemes.desc: Short open back unrounded [ɑ], stressed as the first syllable of every Old Norse word; brief, not the long á.
Alveolar nasal [n] followed by a fully voiced stop [d]; in runic carving the d would be written with the t-rune, which underspecifies voicing.
Voiced labiodental [v] as in English 'very', a second short [ɑ], trilled [r], and a short close [i]; the name is a weak masculine and carries no added nominative -r.

pronunciation.approximation: 'AHND-vah-ri' — three even syllables, stress on the first, the v soft as in 'very', the r trilled, the ending a short 'ih' as in 'bit'.

kin.label: Old Norse
kin.form: Andvari, the dwarf of Andvarafors; beside the proper name stands the common noun andvari, 'care, solicitude, watchfulness'.

kin.label: Younger Futhark
kin.form: ᛅᚾᛏᚢᛅᚱᛁ (a-n-t-u-a-r-i) — the sixteen-rune Viking-Age rendering, with ᛏ writing the voiced d and ᚢ writing v.

kin.label: Modern Icelandic
kin.form: Andvari — the name revived as the title of the learned journal of the Icelandic Literary Society, founded 1874.

pronunciation.note: Andvari is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — no diacritic, no distinctive letter — so the ASCII alphabet loses nothing in copying it. The dwarf's fame rides on his ring, not on his orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Dwarf, Guardian of Gold
domains.subtitle: The Careful One of the Waterfall
domains.lead: Andvari is the dwarf who lived in the waterfall Andvarafors in a pike's shape, sweeping his gold about him with his fins — the most careful hoarder in the northern corpus, and the owner of the ring Andvaranaut. When Loki caught him in Rán's net and stripped him of everything to pay the otter's ransom, Andvari spoke the curse that made his gold a death sentence for every hand that held it after him: Hreiðmarr, Fáfnir, Sigurðr, and the whole line of the Gjúkungar.

cards.name: Andvarafors
cards.desc: The waterfall that was his hall — the stream where he swam in a pike's shape and kept his gold, named for him in Reginsmál's prose.

cards.name: Andvaranaut
cards.desc: 'Andvari's jewel' — the last ring of the hoard, hidden in his hand, taken by force, and answered with the curse that every owner would find death in it.

cards.name: Rán's Net
cards.desc: The sea-queen's net that Loki borrowed to drag the waterfall — the tool that turned a fishing into an extortion.

cards.name: The Pike-Shape
cards.desc: The fish-form in which he swept his hoard through the water — the careful one's disguise, netted all the same.

symbols.name: Andvaranaut
symbols.meaning: The ring taken last and cursed first — a treasure that kills every hand it passes through

symbols.name: Andvarafors
symbols.meaning: The waterfall named for its keeper — a hoard-hall that flows and cannot be locked

symbols.name: Rán's net
symbols.meaning: Borrowed catching-power — the gods paying a blood-debt with a fisherman's trick

symbols.name: The pike-shape
symbols.meaning: The disguise of the careful — a form made for guarding, not for fighting

symbols.name: The otter's ransom
symbols.meaning: The wergild that had to cover a dead otter's skin from the inside — gold counted out hair by hair

mythology.lead: Andvari's dossier is a single episode and its long echo: one afternoon's extortion at a waterfall, and a curse that runs through the rest of the Völsung cycle like poison through water. Reginsmál's prose, Snorri's Skáldskaparmál, and Völsunga saga all tell the catching; everything after — Fáfnir's dragon, Sigurðr's sword, the gold sunk in the Rhine — is the curse working itself out.

myths.title: The Otter's Ransom
myths.text:
Óðinn, Loki, and Hœnir were traveling when they came to a waterfall, and there they saw an otter eating a salmon on the bank, its eyes shut. Loki killed it with a stone and boasted of a double catch — otter and fish at one cast. But the otter was Ótr, son of the farmer Hreiðmarr, a shape-shifter who took a pike's or otter's form to fish the falls. That night the gods sought lodging at Hreiðmarr's house and showed their catch; Hreiðmarr called his sons Fáfnir and Reginn, and the three seized the gods and bound them. The wergild was set by the skin itself: the otter's hide was to be filled with red gold, and then covered with gold from the outside until not a hair showed. Óðinn sent Loki to get the gold, and Loki went down to the world of the black-elves to find it where it lay — in the keeping of a dwarf at a waterfall.

Snorri tells the same in Skáldskaparmál as the explanation of gold's kennings: this is why poets call gold the otter's ransom, the forced payment of the Æsir. The episode exists in the tradition to gloss poetry — a myth doing the work of a dictionary.

myths.title: The Net of Rán
myths.text:
Völsunga saga gives the fullest account of the catching. Loki went to Rán, the sea-queen who drowns sailors, and borrowed her net, then came to the waterfall called Andvarafors. There lived the dwarf Andvari, who kept a pike's shape in the water and swept his gold about him, guarding everything. Loki cast the net and caught him, and demanded the ransom: all the gold in the waterfall, or Andvari's head.

The dwarf paid over the hoard — but he kept one ring back, a small thing, hidden in his hand. Loki saw it and took that too, despite Andvari's plea that with the ring kept he could breed gold again and would not beggar himself entirely. Loki answered that one coin would be too many to leave him, and went up out of the water with the whole of it. Reginsmál's prose tells the same catching more briefly: Loki got Rán's net, cast it before the pike, and the dwarf paid the otter's ransom from his own keeping.

myths.title: The Curse on the Ring
myths.text:
Stripped of everything, Andvari did the only thing left to a dwarf with nothing: he spoke. Reginsmál's prose preserves the curse as the tradition's own words: the gold that Gustr had owned — Gustr, 'Gust', the other name the prose gives the dwarf — would be the death of two brothers, and would bring strife to eight of the kin-line — eight ættlingar — and no man would ever have joy of his wealth. Völsunga saga gives the same sentence over the ring itself: it would be the death of every man who owned it.

The ring got a name from its first owner's loss: Andvaranaut, 'Andvari's jewel'. Nothing in the corpus says the curse was magic in the modern sense; it needs none. What the careful one laid on the gold was a prophecy any listener could verify, because the gold itself was now worth killing for — and the story spends the rest of its length proving him right, owner by owner.

myths.title: Fáfnir's Bed of Gold
myths.text:
The gods filled the otter-skin and covered it, and the last hair was covered with Andvaranaut itself — Loki had kept the ring back from Hreiðmarr until that final hair, so that even the last coin of the hoard went into the ransom. The gods went free. But Hreiðmarr refused his sons any share of the gold, and the curse began its work at once: Fáfnir killed his father sleeping, took all the treasure, and refused Reginn a share in turn. He carried the hoard out to the heath called Gnitaheiðr, and there he brooded on it until he became the worst of serpents — a dragon lying on his gold, wearing the helmet of terror.

Reginn, cheated, went to the court of King Hjálprekr and became foster-father to Sigurðr of the Völsung line. He reforged the sword Gram from the shards of Sigmund's blade and egged the young man to the heath. Sigurðr dug a pit in the dragon's path, stabbed up into the belly as Fáfnir crawled over him to drink, and then — warned by the nuthatches that Reginn meant him harm — cut off his foster-father's head. He ate of the dragon's heart and understood the speech of birds; he loaded the hoard, Andvaranaut and all, on Grani's back. The careful one's gold had a new owner, and the third owner of the ring was the greatest hero of the North. The curse did not care.

myths.title: The Gold in the Rhine
myths.text:
From Sigurðr the treasure passed as blood-price and dowry into the house of the Gjúkungar — Gunnar, Högni, and their sister Guðrún, whom Sigurðr married. When Sigurðr was murdered in his bed over Brynhildr's vengeance, the hoard was the Gjúkungs' alone, and it drew King Atli, Brynhildr's brother, who invited his brothers-in-law to his hall to take it from them. Gunnar and Högni rode knowing the invitation was death, and before they crossed the Rhine they did the last careful thing anyone does with Andvari's gold: they sank the whole hoard in the river, in deep water, where no one would have joy of it — the dwarf's sentence carried out by its victims themselves.

Atli's men cut Högni's heart out and cast Gunnar living into a pit of serpents, where he played the harp with his toes until an adder struck him to the heart; the hoard he died to keep lay at the bottom of the Rhine, ownerless. Atlakviða ends the account with the river itself as the treasure's last keeper: the Rhine shall hold the strife-metal of the Niflungar. Two brothers dead, eight princes at strife, no man the happier — Reginsmál's prophecy closed like a hand. Andvari was avenged on everyone, which is to say on no one in particular, which is exactly what a curse is.

lore.syncretism: Andvari needs no foreign counterpart to be understood — the cursed-hoard complex is native Germanic and runs through the whole North: treasure extorted is treasure poisoned. The corpus itself supplies the sharpest contrast in another dwarf-ring: Draupnir, forged freely by [[brokkr|Brokkr]] and [[sindri|Sindri]] for the gods, which drips eight new rings every ninth night — the given ring multiplies, the taken ring kills. Continental heroic tradition keeps the same stratum: the hoard of the Nibelungenlied, sunk in the Rhine and deadly to its holders, is the southern telling of the Andvaranaut complex, and scholars from Lindow onward treat the Norse and German versions as one inheritance rather than borrowings. The dwarf caught in fish-shape also has a family resemblance to the water-spirits of later folklore, but the Eddic Andvari is a smith and hoarder first; his pike-form is camouflage, not nature.
lore.culturalLegacy: Andvari's afterlife is one of the largest in all mythology, under another name. Wagner's Alberich in Das Rheingold — the dwarf of the water's depth who is robbed of his gold, lays a curse on the ring forged from it, and watches it destroy owner after owner through four operas — is built substantially on the Andvari of Reginsmál and Völsunga saga, crossed with the Nibelungenlied's hoard; the curse-motif that drives the entire Ring cycle is the sentence spoken at Andvarafors. William Morris's Sigurd the Volsung (1876) kept the original name before English readers, and the Nibelungenlied's Rhine-gold carried the same hoard into German memory. In Iceland the name itself was revived with no curse attached: Andvari is the title of the learned journal of the Icelandic Literary Society, founded in 1874 — the careful one finally keeping something that multiplies without killing. Modern fantasy's treasury of cursed gold, from dragons' hoards onward, runs downhill from his waterfall.
lore.extendedMeditation: His name is care itself — andvari, watchfulness, the quality of mind that checks the locks twice. And the myth is merciless to it: the most careful keeper in the corpus is caught in an afternoon, by a borrowed net, in his own water, and stripped to the last hidden ring. Care could not save him, because care guards against theft and what came for him was law — a wergild, a debt, a skin that had to be covered hair by hair. What he had left was speech, and he used it like a dwarf: precisely, vindictively, and with perfect aim. The curse is the one thing he made that nobody could take, because it was already given. Everything after is arithmetic — two brothers, eight princes, no joy — and the myth lets the numbers run for four generations to teach a single lesson the North never tired of: gold that is taken by force does not change owners; it changes victims. Andvari in his waterfall is the small still beginning of the Völsung tragedy, the moment the hook was set. The careful one's revenge on the careless world was simply to tell it the truth about what it had just picked up.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Norse form is Andvari — already plain ASCII, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover; in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᛅᚾᛏᚢᛅᚱᛁ (a-n-t-u-a-r-i, the t-rune writing d and úr writing v). Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered in the ordinary way: andvari.com is held outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Andvari himself is a purely literary figure: no runestone, votive deposit, or named image records him. But the cycle his gold sets in motion is the best-attested narrative in Viking-Age art. The Ramsund carving in Södermanland (Sö 101, c. 1030) cuts the whole Fáfnir episode into a rock face — Sigurðr thrusting up through the serpent's body, the slain Reginn with his smith's tools, Grani loaded with the treasure, and the birds whose speech the dragon-heart taught — and the Gök stone (Sö 327) weaves the same scenes through a runic inscription. The Drävle runestone (U 1163) shows Sigurðr stabbing the serpent, and related scenes appear on the Isle of Man and in English stone sculpture as far west as the Halton cross in Lancashire, tracking the cycle along the Norse sea-roads. The manuscript witnesses are thin in the usual way: Reginsmál and its narrative prose stand in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda, Snorri's account in the codices of the Prose Edda, and Völsunga saga in the paper manuscript NKS 1824 b 4to (c. 1400), the saga's only complete medieval copy.
